title.en: Jensen Huang scandal illustrates why human nature is cybersecurity’s weakest link

hook.en: The end of Jensen Huang’s tenure at Nvidia is steeped in irony. The chief executive of a company whose growth has been propelled by the seemingly unstoppable rise of artificial intelligence was brought down by a vulnerability that no algorithm can eliminate: human nature.

sections.body_en: Huang’s resignation from the chipmaker he co-founded followed reports of multiple affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a business executive whom U.S. authorities suspect of spying for China. The company says no secrets were leaked. In 2023, Italian Premier Giorgia Meloni spoke candidly about foreign affairs in a call with Russian pranksters who recorded and released the conversation. In 2011, former CIA Director David Petraeus gave his biographer, with whom he was having an affair, access to notebooks containing classified information. **Social cues** that increase a sense of familiarity and intimacy make people feel safer and more willing to divulge information.

sections.heading_en: The comfort of a human voice
sections.body_en: Kevin Mitnick gained access to privileged information at companies such as Nokia and Motorola before his arrest in 1995 by having conversations with his targets rather than writing sophisticated code-breaking software. He called people up and talked them into handing over passwords by claiming to be the new IT guy or a boss’s colleague. Hearing a person’s voice makes that person seem more capable and relatable than reading their written thoughts. In a study conducted with social psychologist Mahdi Roghanizad, participants received about twice as many “yes” responses to favors over the phone as they did by email. A human voice may be all you need to obtain company secrets or circumvent export laws.

Studies have found that human touch can also have surprising effects on tipping behavior, acquiescence and risk-taking.

In a famous 1984 study, a server who lightly touched diners as she handed them their change received bigger tips. In another classic psychology study, female experimenters approached 178 strangers and asked them for change to use a nearby pay phone. When the experimenters lightly touched the arm of a person they approached, that person was 76% more likely to agree to give the change.

The researchers theorized that these light touches created a sense of familiarity. That familiarity, in turn, made people more willing to open their wallets.

Other research suggests that light touch can also make people feel safer and more willing to take risks. In a 2010 study, participants were more willing to take financial risks when a female experimenter gave them a light, comforting pat on their shoulder.

Perhaps the most well-known study of influence, Stanley Milgram’s infamous shock experiment, illustrates how much it can matter to be in the room when you ask someone to do something they may be feeling uneasy about.

In the original study, an experimenter stood behind participants and instructed them to administer purportedly dangerous shocks to someone they thought was just another participant. The experimenter asked participants to incrementally increase the intensity of the shocks. Nearly two-thirds of participants went all the way to the highest shock setting. In a variation of the study, however, the experimenter left the room and gave instructions over the phone. In this version, only 22.5% went that far.

Although researchers continue to debate how to interpret Milgram’s findings, my colleagues and I have similarly found that people are far more likely to say yes when we ask them to do something face-to-face.

In one study, participants who made requests in person were 34 times more likely to get a yes than those who made requests by email. In another study, in-person requests were significantly more effective than requests made over the phone or video call.

Cyberattacks and phishing emails pose real threats to security. But sometimes the biggest threats come from the people in the room with you. While we don’t know exactly what transpired between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, her proximity to the Nvidia CEO illustrates a vulnerability that even the best cybersecurity measures can struggle to guard against.

summary.vi: Vụ việc liên quan đến Jensen Huang minh họa cách bản chất con người trở thành điểm yếu trong an ninh mạng. Dù công nghệ bảo mật phát triển, các mối quan hệ xã hội, giọng nói quen thuộc và sự tiếp xúc thể xác vẫn tạo ra lòng tin dễ bị lợi dụng. Các nghiên cứu tâm lý chỉ ra con người dễ đồng ý hơn khi giao tiếp trực tiếp hoặc qua điện thoại.
summary.fr: La chute de Jensen Huang chez Nvidia met en lumière une faille majeure : la nature humaine. Malgré des outils de protection sophistiqués, les individus restent vulnérables aux interactions directes. Qu’il s’agisse d’une voix familière au téléphone, d’un léger contact physique ou d’une présence en face-à-face, ces signaux sociaux augmentent la confiance et incitent à baisser la garde. Les recherches en psychologie montrent que la persuasion fonctionne mieux ainsi, contournant les protocoles de sécurité les plus stricts.
summary.de: Der Fall von Jensen Huang zeigt, wie anfällig selbst mächtige Organisationen für menschliche Manipulation sind. Obwohl Künstliche Intelligenz boomt, bleibt der Mensch das schwächste Glied in der Sicherheitskette. Studien belegen, dass persönliche Nähe, eine menschliche Stimme oder eine sanfte Berührung unser Vertrauen drastisch erhöhen und uns zu riskanten Handlungen verleiten können. Soziale Beeinflussung umgeht oft jede digitale Firewall, da wir evolutionär darauf programmiert sind, auf soziale Signale positiv zu reagieren.
summary.es: La dimisión de Jensen Huang en Nvidia demuestra que la ciberseguridad a menudo flaquea por el factor humano. Aunque la tecnología protege los datos contra ataques digitales avanzados, las personas siguen siendo vulnerables a la manipulación interpersonal. Elementos como la voz humana, el contacto físico sutil y la interacción cara a cara generan una falsa sensación de confianza y familiaridad. Diversos experimentos psicológicos confirman que estas señales sociales aumentan drásticamente la probabilidad de que alguien ceda información confidencial o tome riesgos innecesarios. En definitiva, la naturaleza humana representa el eslabón más débil en la seguridad de cualquier organización.

keyPoint.en: Security is like a fortress with an open gate made of flesh and bone. Human nature always seeks connection, trusting familiar voices and gentle touches over cold logic. When you face a request for sensitive information, pause and ask: would I trust this person if they were sending me an email instead?
keyPoint.vi: Bảo mật giống như một pháo đài có cổng mở làm bằng da thịt. Bản chất con người luôn tìm kiếm sự kết nối, tin tưởng những giọng nói quen thuộc và cái chạm nhẹ nhàng hơn là logic lạnh lùng. Khi bạn đối mặt với một yêu cầu thông tin nhạy cảm, hãy dừng lại và tự hỏi: liệu mình có tin tưởng người này nếu họ gửi email thay vì gọi điện?

en: Verify the identity of anyone asking for sensitive data through an official secondary channel.
Pause for ten seconds before complying with urgent requests made over phone or in person.
Report any suspicious social engineering attempts to your security team immediately.
vi: Xác minh danh tính của bất kỳ ai yêu cầu dữ liệu nhạy cảm thông qua kênh phụ chính thức.
Dừng lại mười giây trước khi tuân thủ các yêu cầu khẩn cấp qua điện thoại hoặc trực tiếp.
Báo cáo ngay mọi nỗ lực thao túng xã hội đáng ngờ cho nhóm bảo mật của bạn.

en.jensen huang: The chief executive of Nvidia whose tenure ended amid a scandal.
en.nvidia: A major technology company specializing in artificial intelligence chips.
en.alice huang: A business executive suspected by U.S. authorities of spying for China.
en.kevin mitnick: An infamous hacker known for exploiting human psychology over technical code.
en.giorgia meloni: Italian Premier who was recorded speaking candidly with Russian pranksters.
en.david petraeus: Former CIA Director who shared classified notebooks with his biographer.
en.mahdi roghanizad: A social psychologist who co-conducted communication channel studies.
en.stanley milgram: Psychologist known for his infamous shock experiment on obedience and influence.
